title: The Cocoa Bean That Travelled the World

pages.text: Under the cool canopy of tall forest shade trees near Sefwi Wiawso, ten-year-old Adwoa walked with her parents after Saturday breakfast. Golden-yellow cocoa pods grew directly out of the trunks and thick branches of the cocoa trees—a botanical wonder called cauliflory. ‘Papa,’ Adwoa asked, ‘how does a wet white seed inside this pod become a smooth brown bar of chocolate in shops around the world?’
sentences: Under the cool canopy of tall forest shade trees near Sefwi Wiawso, ten-year-old Adwoa walked with her parents after Saturday breakfast.
Golden-yellow cocoa pods grew directly out of the trunks and thick branches of the cocoa trees—a botanical wonder called cauliflory.
‘Papa,’ Adwoa asked, ‘how does a wet white seed inside this pod become a smooth brown bar of chocolate in shops around the world?’
pages.alt: Ten-year-old Adwoa walks with Papa Kofi and Mama Efua beneath tall shade trees where golden cocoa pods grow on the tree trunks.

pages.text: Papa Kofi pointed to the tall terminalia and plantain trees shading the cocoa grove. ‘Great chocolate starts with sustainable farming,’ he said. ‘Shade trees protect the soil, hold moisture and give birds a home. And on a responsible Ghanaian cocoa farm, children go to school and never use sharp cutlasses, spray chemicals or carry heavy loads. Grown-up workers harvest the ripe pods carefully so the tree bark cushions can flower again next season.’
sentences: Papa Kofi pointed to the tall terminalia and plantain trees shading the cocoa grove.
‘Great chocolate starts with sustainable farming,’ he said.
‘Shade trees protect the soil, hold moisture and give birds a home.
And on a responsible Ghanaian cocoa farm, children go to school and never use sharp cutlasses, spray chemicals or carry heavy loads.
Grown-up workers harvest the ripe pods carefully so the tree bark cushions can flower again next season.’
pages.alt: Adult farm workers carefully harvest golden cocoa pods while Adwoa sketches the shade trees and birds from a safe path.

pages.text: At the farm fermentation spot, adult workers split the thick yellow pods with wooden mallets and scooped out the sweet, white, mucilage-covered cocoa beans. ‘Wait—they are white and taste fruity like soursop, not like chocolate at all!’ Adwoa exclaimed. Mama Efua laughed. ‘Raw cocoa beans have no chocolate flavour yet. We heap them on clean plantain leaves and cover them for six days of fermentation.’
sentences: At the farm fermentation spot, adult workers split the thick yellow pods with wooden mallets and scooped out the sweet, white, mucilage-covered cocoa beans.
‘Wait—they are white and taste fruity like soursop, not like chocolate at all!’ Adwoa exclaimed.
Mama Efua laughed.
‘Raw cocoa beans have no chocolate flavour yet.
We heap them on clean plantain leaves and cover them for six days of fermentation.’
pages.alt: Adult workers heap white cocoa beans onto broad green plantain leaves while Adwoa observes the white pulp.

pages.text: ‘During those six days,’ Mama Efua explained, ‘natural microscopic yeasts and bacteria feed on the sugary white pulp, warming the heap to nearly fifty degrees Celsius. Chemical reactions inside the bean reduce bitterness and create the rich flavour precursors of chocolate!’ Next, the brown fermented beans were spread on raised raffia mats in the sun and turned by hand for seven to ten days until their moisture dropped below eight percent.

Chemical reactions inside the bean reduce bitterness and create the rich flavour precursors of chocolate!’ Next, the brown fermented beans were spread on raised raffia mats in the sun and turned by hand for seven to ten days until their moisture dropped below eight percent.
pages.alt: Adwoa watches her parents turn rich brown cocoa beans drying on raised bamboo and raffia mats in the sunshine.

pages.text: At the cooperative society shed, a licensed Quality Control officer cut open sample beans to check that they were thoroughly fermented, dry and free of mould or slate defects before sealing the jute sacks. ‘Ghanaian cocoa is famous worldwide for high quality,’ Papa Kofi said proudly. ‘Yet for decades, most of our beans were shipped overseas raw, while factories in other countries turned them into expensive chocolates.’

‘Yet for decades, most of our beans were shipped overseas raw, while factories in other countries turned them into expensive chocolates.’
pages.alt: In a tidy cocoa buying shed, a quality control officer inspects cut cocoa beans on a tray beside stacked jute sacks.

pages.text: During the school holidays, Adwoa’s cooperative visited a Ghanaian cocoa-processing and chocolate factory in Tema, where Auntie Baaba, a food scientist, welcomed them in a white coat and hairnet. ‘Here in Ghana, we add value to our own beans!’ Auntie Baaba said. First, giant machines cleaned and roasted the beans to deepen their aroma, then cracked and winnowed away the thin shells to leave crunchy roasted pieces called cocoa nibs.
sentences: During the school holidays, Adwoa’s cooperative visited a Ghanaian cocoa-processing and chocolate factory in Tema, where Auntie Baaba, a food scientist, welcomed them in a white coat and hairnet.
‘Here in Ghana, we add value to our own beans!’ Auntie Baaba said.
First, giant machines cleaned and roasted the beans to deepen their aroma, then cracked and winnowed away the thin shells to leave crunchy roasted pieces called cocoa nibs.
pages.alt: Inside a spotless Ghanaian chocolate factory in Tema, Auntie Baaba in a white lab coat shows Adwoa roasted cocoa beans and cocoa nibs.

pages.text: Next, heavy rollers ground the warm cocoa nibs into a thick dark liquid called cocoa liquor—which contains zero alcohol, only natural cocoa solids and cocoa butter! Huge hydraulic presses squeezed part of the cocoa liquor into golden cocoa butter for chocolates and skin creams, and fine cocoa powder for drinks. In the chocolate hall, cocoa liquor, extra cocoa butter, sugar and milk were mixed, refined and stirred for hours in a warm machine called a conche.
sentences: Next, heavy rollers ground the warm cocoa nibs into a thick dark liquid called cocoa liquor—which contains zero alcohol, only natural cocoa solids and cocoa butter!
Huge hydraulic presses squeezed part of the cocoa liquor into golden cocoa butter for chocolates and skin creams, and fine cocoa powder for drinks.
In the chocolate hall, cocoa liquor, extra cocoa butter, sugar and milk were mixed, refined and stirred for hours in a warm machine called a conche.
pages.alt: Adwoa looks through a glass window at stainless-steel conching machines stirring smooth, glossy liquid chocolate.

pages.text: ‘Why does a finished box of chocolates sell for much more than the raw beans inside it?’ Adwoa asked, opening her notebook. Auntie Baaba drew an illustrative classroom chart on the whiteboard. ‘Suppose, in a simple training example, a workshop buys 10 kilograms of dried cocoa beans for 300 cedis. After roasting, grinding, adding sugar, milk and foil wrappers, paying factory workers and electricity, and chilling the bars, the workshop produces 100 bars that sell for 12 cedis each—1,200 cedis in total retail sales.’
sentences: ‘Why does a finished box of chocolates sell for much more than the raw beans inside it?’ Adwoa asked, opening her notebook.
Auntie Baaba drew an illustrative classroom chart on the whiteboard.
‘Suppose, in a simple training example, a workshop buys 10 kilograms of dried cocoa beans for 300 cedis.

After roasting, grinding, adding sugar, milk and foil wrappers, paying factory workers and electricity, and chilling the bars, the workshop produces 100 bars that sell for 12 cedis each—1,200 cedis in total retail sales.’
pages.alt: Auntie Baaba explains a visual value-chain chart showing raw beans, factory processing, packaging, cooling and retail bars.

pages.text: ‘Does the chocolate maker keep all 900 cedis of the difference as profit?’ Adwoa asked sharply. ‘Good catch!’ Auntie Baaba smiled. ‘No! In our illustrative example, if sugar, milk, food-grade packaging, FDA testing, cold storage, worker wages and transport cost 700 cedis, then total production cost is 300 plus 700 equals 1,000 cedis—leaving 200 cedis in net profit. Value addition is real work: quality, food safety, branding and reliable distribution all cost money and skill—and keep skilled jobs here in Ghana!’

Value addition is real work: quality, food safety, branding and reliable distribution all cost money and skill—and keep skilled jobs here in Ghana!’
pages.alt: Adwoa checks the subtraction in her notebook while factory staff pack foil-wrapped Ghanaian chocolate bars into chilled boxes.

pages.text: On the bus ride home, Adwoa savoured a square of dark Ghanaian chocolate and wrote at the bottom of her page: What Would You Build, Discover or Change? ‘One day I want to help our cooperative process cocoa butter, natural soaps and export-quality chocolates right in our district,’ she told Papa Kofi and Mama Efua. Look around your town or region—what local crop or raw material could you process, package or improve to create more value in Ghana?

activities.question: Why do cocoa farmers ferment wet cocoa beans under plantain leaves for six days before drying them?
options: Microbes break down pulp and trigger reactions that build chocolate aroma
To paint the beans bright blue
To make the beans sprout into new trees inside the sack
activities.explanation: Fermentation by natural yeasts and bacteria heats the heap and forms the chemical flavour precursors needed for real chocolate aroma.

activities.definition: Separated the lighter cracked outer shells from the roasted cocoa nibs using air currents
distractors: Frozen inside a block of ice

activities.question: In Auntie Baaba’s illustrative workshop example (300 cedis beans + 700 cedis processing/packaging = 1,000 cedis total cost; 100 bars sold at 12 cedis = 1,200 cedis), what is the net profit?
options: 200 cedis (1,200 cedis revenue minus 1,000 cedis total cost)
1,200 cedis because processing and packaging are free
900 cedis because workers and electricity cost nothing
activities.explanation: Total cost is 300 + 700 = 1,000 cedis. Subtracting 1,000 cedis from 1,200 cedis in revenue leaves 200 cedis net profit.

activities.prompt: Put the stages of the cocoa value chain in order from farm to finished bar.
items: Harvesting ripe pods, fermenting beans for 6 days and sun-drying on mats.
Quality grading, roasting and winnowing beans into cocoa nibs.
Grinding nibs into cocoa liquor, pressing cocoa butter and conching chocolate.

activities.prompt: What Would You Build, Discover or Change? How does processing raw crops into finished products in Ghana help both farmers and young graduates?
